summary: In this episode, the hosts explore the concept of the Millennium in Christian theology, focusing on Revelation 20. They begin by examining the biblical notion of an 'age' (Greek: aeon), showing how it refers not just to a period of time but to a distinct world order or state of things. They trace the various ages in Scripture, from creation to the post-exilic period, and discuss the transition points between them, particularly the coming of the Messiah and the inauguration of the Messianic Age. The hosts argue that the Messianic Age is not a future earthly utopia but is the current age in which Christ reigns from heaven, ruling in the midst of His enemies until the final judgment. They critique both ancient chiliasm (premillennialism) and modern dispensationalism for projecting this age into the future and for misunderstanding the nature of the kingdom. They also address the common claim that St. Irenaeus was a chiliast, arguing that the evidence does not support this. The episode concludes with an exhortation to live joyfully and hopefully in the present Messianic Age, participating in Christ's victory over the powers of evil.

entities.title: St. Augustine
entities.summary: Bishop of Hippo (354-430) whose work 'City of God' developed the concept of the 'secular' as a world order, influencing Western eschatology and the understanding of ages.

entities.title: Joachim of Fiore
entities.summary: 12th-century Italian mystic who proposed a tripartite division of history into ages of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, predicting a future utopian age of the Spirit. His ideas influenced later millenarian movements.

entities.title: St. Irenaeus
entities.summary: 2nd-century bishop and Church Father, known for his work 'Against Heresies.' Often claimed as a chiliast, but the hosts argue the evidence does not support this, as his writings affirm the bodily resurrection and the present reality of the kingdom.

entities.title: Montanus
entities.summary: Founder of Montanism, a 2nd-century heretical movement that claimed new prophecy and was chiliastic. His association with chiliasm contributed to its condemnation.

entities.title: Daniel (Prophet)
entities.summary: Old Testament prophet whose visions, particularly in Daniel 7, describe the succession of world empires and the enthronement of the Son of Man, foundational for understanding the Messianic Age.

entities.title: Revelation 20
entities.summary: The primary biblical passage about the Millennium, describing the binding of Satan for a thousand years, the reign of the martyrs with Christ, and the final rebellion of Gog and Magog.

concepts.title: Age (Aeon)
concepts.summary: The concept of an 'age' in Scripture, often translated from the Greek 'aeon' or Hebrew 'yom' (day), refers to a distinct period characterized by a particular world order or state of things, not merely a measure of time.

concepts.title: Day of the Lord
concepts.summary: A pivotal transitional moment in Scripture when God intervenes in history to judge and inaugurate a new age. It is often associated with the Hebrew 'yom Yahweh' and is seen as a time of both judgment and deliverance.

concepts.title: Messianic Age
concepts.summary: The age inaugurated by the coming of the Messiah, in which Christ reigns from heaven over the nations, ruling in the midst of His enemies until the final judgment. This age is identified as the present period of the Church.

concepts.title: New Covenant
concepts.summary: The covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel, characterized by the internalization of God's law and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, enabling believers to fulfill the righteous requirements of the Torah.

concepts.title: Chiliasm (Millenarianism)
concepts.summary: An early Christian belief that the Messianic Age would be a future, literal thousand-year earthly reign of Christ, often associated with material abundance. It was condemned by the Church as an eschatological error.

concepts.title: First Resurrection
concepts.summary: In Revelation 20, the 'first resurrection' refers to the spiritual resurrection of the souls of the righteous, who reign with Christ during the Messianic Age, not a bodily resurrection before a future millennium.

claims.text: The millennium of Revelation 20 is not a future earthly reign but the present Messianic Age, in which Christ rules from heaven over the nations, with Satan bound and the saints reigning with Him.
Chiliasm, the belief in a future literal thousand-year earthly reign of Christ, was condemned by the Church as an eschatological error, though it is not a Christological or Trinitarian heresy.
St. Irenaeus was not a chiliast; the passages often cited to prove this actually affirm the bodily resurrection and the present reality of the kingdom, not a future earthly millennium.
The New Covenant does not abolish the Torah but internalizes it, with the Holy Spirit empowering believers to fulfill the righteous requirements of the law.
Dispensationalism errs by inserting a 'church age' between the great tribulation and the Messianic Age, whereas the New Testament identifies the present age as the Messianic Age.

scriptural_links.summary: The central passage on the Millennium, interpreted as describing the binding of Satan and the reign of the martyrs during the present Messianic Age.

Describes the enthronement of the Son of Man and the giving of dominion to the saints, while the beasts' lives are prolonged for a season, indicating a period between the Messiah's enthronement and final judgment.
Quoted in the New Testament to show that the Messiah rules in the midst of His enemies until they are made His footstool, supporting the idea of a present Messianic Age.
The promise of a New Covenant with Israel and Judah, characterized by the law written on hearts and universal knowledge of God, fulfilled in the Messianic Age.
Prophecy of the outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, quoted at Pentecost, linking the Messianic Age with the day of the Lord.
Describes the peaceable kingdom where animals coexist, symbolizing the reordering of creation in the Messianic Age.

glossary.definition: A period of time characterized by a particular world order or state of things; often translated as 'age' in English.
The belief in a future literal thousand-year earthly reign of Christ, derived from the Greek word 'chilioi' (thousand).
A Protestant theological system that divides history into distinct dispensations or periods, often emphasizing a future earthly millennium and a separate plan for Israel.
A Latin term for 'age' or 'world order,' used by St. Augustine to describe the succession of worldly ages in contrast to the eternal city of God.
In Revelation 20, the spiritual resurrection of the souls of the righteous, who reign with Christ during the Messianic Age.
